passage:
The messages came at night, from an account with no photo and a string of numbers for a name. "Nobody likes you." "Quit the choir." Binita read each one twice in her room in Guwahati, and by midnight she had a list: the girl who lost the solo, the boy who mocked her accent, her old lab partner. She couldn't eat or study; the guessing consumed her.
On the phone, Divyansh said, "It doesn't matter who it is right now. Save everything. Screenshot the lot."
In the morning they showed the pages to the choir teacher, reported the account to the app, and the teacher told the school. Binita felt lighter for the first time in days. She still glanced at people, wondering, but she pushed the list into a drawer.

qa.q: Which three people were on Binita's list?
qa.a: The list had the girl who lost the solo, the boy who mocked her accent and her old lab partner.

qa.q: Why couldn't Binita eat or study that night?
qa.a: The guessing about who sent the messages consumed her and the hurtful words kept replaying, so she felt anxious and hurt.

qa.q: What steps did Binita and Divyansh take, and why did they matter?
qa.a: They saved screenshots, reported the account to the app and told the choir teacher, who told the school; this keeps evidence and brings adults in, so Binita doesn't have to solve the puzzle alone.

qa.q: How might Divyansh see Binita's list of suspects?
qa.a: Divyansh probably sees a worried friend spiralling, and believes that saving evidence and reporting matter more than knowing who it is.

grounding: Shows a teen receiving anonymous nasty messages, obsessing over who, then preserving evidence and reporting.

passage:
Okay, you want to know about the anonymous account? I'm Gargi. It started in February. An account with no photo, called "truthteller_x," sent me messages every night. "Everyone laughs at you." "Nobody wants you in the group." Stuff about my weight.

The worst part wasn't even the words. It was the guessing. I lay awake going through every name. Was it the girls from dance? My old best friend? I even started to suspect Gurleen, who has been nothing but kind to me. I was checking everyone's face at school for clues.

Gurleen noticed I was acting weird and asked. I told her, and I told her I'd suspected her. She wasn't even offended. She said, "Stop guessing. Let's give it to someone who can actually find out."

So we screenshotted every message, reported the account on the app, and that same day I showed my mother and our school counsellor. The account was taken down in a week.

I still don't know who it was. And I've decided I'm okay not knowing.

qa.q: What was the anonymous account called?
What was Gargi feeling while guessing who was behind the account?
qa.a: Gargi felt anxious and consumed, lying awake suspecting everyone, even kind friends like Gurleen.

qa.q: What did Gargi and Gurleen do that was wise?
qa.a: They saved screenshots, reported the account and told Gargi's mother and the school counsellor that same day, instead of guessing.

qa.q: How did Gurleen react when she learned Gargi had suspected her?
qa.a: Gurleen was not offended; she understood and helped Gargi stop guessing and get help.

grounding: It shows a teen targeted by an anonymous account who becomes consumed by guessing who it is, then preserves evidence, reports to the platform and school, and lets go of guessing.

passage:
Monday. The messages started coming to Anirban from an account with no name and no picture. "Loser." "Your voice is so annoying." "Quit the debate team." He read them twenty times. By night he was sure it was Rafiq, who had lost the debate spot to him.

Wednesday. Anirban barely slept. In class he watched Rafiq's every move, looking for proof. He drafted a message to Rafiq: "I know it's you." His finger hovered. Then he thought: what if it isn't? He'd be doing to Rafiq what the account was doing to him.

He deleted the draft. Instead he saved every message with the time, reported the account on the app, and that evening showed his father. Papa emailed the school counsellor at once.

The next Monday. The counsellor had involved the school's IT teacher, and the account had been removed. Anirban still didn't know who it was. But in debate practice, Rafiq said, "Good point," and Anirban realised he'd been ready to accuse the wrong person.

qa.q: Who did Anirban suspect was behind the account?
qa.a: Anirban suspected Rafiq, who had lost the debate spot to him.

qa.q: What was Anirban feeling on Wednesday?
qa.a: Anirban felt anxious and suspicious, barely sleeping and watching Rafiq for proof.

qa.q: What did Anirban do instead of sending the accusation, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Anirban saved the messages, reported the account and told his father, which got the school involved and stopped him accusing someone without proof.

qa.q: What would have happened to Rafiq if Anirban had sent the draft?
qa.a: Rafiq might have been hurt and falsely accused, feeling bullied in the same way Anirban was.

grounding: It shows a teen receiving nasty anonymous messages who obsesses over who sent them, then preserves evidence, reports to the platform and school, and stops guessing.
